title: Three More Charged in Laredo Rail Yard Case, Bringing Total to 14
excerpt: Federal prosecutors have charged three more people in the case of seven migrants who died inside a shipping container found at Union Pacific's Laredo rail yard in May, bringing the total charged to 14, the Justice Department said.
content:
Federal prosecutors have charged three more people in the case of seven migrants who died inside a freight container found at Union Pacific's rail yard in Laredo in May, bringing the total number of defendants to 14, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.

The three newly charged defendants, all from Honduras, are Juan Alvaro Membreno-Contreras, 40; Yuri Julissa Cuaresma Paredes, 34; and Mavis Aleyda Escalante Peraza, 38, according to the department. They join 11 people indicted in July. A federal grand jury in the Western District of Texas returned the superseding indictment Nov. 9.

Seven migrants crossed near Del Rio on May 9 and were taken to the Union Pacific tracks there, where smugglers used bolt cutters to remove the lock from a container on a stopped train and shut them inside, according to the department. The container sat atop a second container, had no ventilation or air conditioning, and its door was fastened from the outside so the migrants could not get out. Outdoor temperatures that day were between 88 and 92 degrees.

The train headed east to San Antonio, where the smugglers allegedly opened the door, saw the migrants were in trouble and ran, according to the department. One person who had died was left by the tracks there, and the others stayed in the container as the train continued south to Laredo. On May 10, a worker at the Laredo rail yard spotted a leg jutting from the container, and officers found six people dead inside.

Of the seven who died, four came from Mexico and three from Honduras, including a 14-year-old, according to the department. Prosecutors said one or more of the migrants sent a plea for help to someone close to them.

The department said the smuggling ring was active from at least April 2023 until May 12, 2026, moving migrants deeper into the country on cargo trains after they were brought across the border from Mexico. Payments from migrants or their relatives and friends ranged from $1,500 to $10,000, according to the department.

Twelve defendants face charges tied to the deaths, which could bring life in prison, and the new filing also adds counts including conspiracy to commit money laundering, according to the department. Eleven defendants face the money laundering conspiracy count, punishable by up to 20 years. The department said four of the 14 defendants are U.S. citizens, three are noncitizens and seven are in the country illegally.

An indictment is only an accusation. Each defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty in court.

Sources: U.S. Department of Justice, Nov. 9, 2026; KEDT, Nov. 10, 2026; Local National, Nov. 16, 2026.
